<div class="callout-note" role="note">
<p>Identification Standards are technical and intended for practitioners working in identification management.</p>
<p>If you’re new to this area, you can develop your skills and capability through the guidance and training options available under <a href="https://www.digital.govt.nz/standards-and-guidance/identity/identification-management">Identification management</a>.</p>
</div>
<h2>Application of this standard</h2>
<p>This standard applies whenever assurance is needed that the current request is being made by the original Entity – in other words, that the returning Entity is the same Entity that was initially enrolled.</p>
<p>While this standard is primarily targeted at Relying Parties (RP), it is also applicable to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Credential Providers establishing an Authenticator for a Credential, and</li>
<li>Facilitation Providers establishing an Authenticator for a facilitation mechanism.</li>
</ul>
<p>All parties are accountable for the controls stated in this standard, even if they have employed or contracted aspects to other parties.</p>
<p>Application of the controls in this standard will contribute to the reduction of identity fraud by reducing the ability for unauthorised entities to gain access to the information and entitlements belonging to an enrolled entity.</p>
<p>The scope of the requirements in this standard is explicitly related to the use of Authenticators and the process of authentication. It does not include considerations for security, messaging methods, or other implementation matters, such as steps to detect unauthorised authentication events using analytics and behaviour measures that are not part of an Authenticator.</p>
<p>For more information on the interpretation of each control and how it can be applied, see the related implementation guide.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.digital.govt.nz/standards-and-guidance/identification-standards/implementing-the-authentication-assurance-standard">Implementing the Authentication Assurance Standard</a></p>
<h3>Effective date and versions</h3>
<p>This standard is effective from <time datetime="2026-05-01">1 May 2026</time> and replaces the earlier versions.</p>
<p><strong>Version 3</strong> (current version) — clarifies use of a biometric at level 3 and the integrity of link between binding and authentication.</p>
<p><strong>Version 2</strong> (effective <time datetime="2024-10-01">1 October 2024</time>) — incorporates the controls from the Binding Assurance Standard relating to binding consistency and control of Authenticators by Entities, regroups and reorders controls and makes some simplifications.</p>
<p><strong>Version 1</strong> (effective 1 March 2021) — first published version of the standard.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.dia.govt.nz/diawebsite.nsf/wpg_URL/Resource-material-Evidence-of-Identity-Standard-Index?OpenDocument">Historic versions of the Identification Standards — Department of Internal Affairs</a></p>
<h2>Before applying this standard</h2>
<h3>Authenticator types</h3>
<p>Interpretation of this standard assumes a strong understanding of the 3 authentication factor types:</p>
<ul>
<li>something the Authenticator holder knows — knowledge factor</li>
<li>something the Authenticator holder has — possession factor</li>
<li>something the Authenticator holder is or does — biometric factor</li>
</ul>
<p>along with good knowledge about the characteristics of the entities to whom the service or transaction has been offered. See the <a href="https://www.digital.govt.nz/standards-and-guidance/identity/identification-management/guidance/guide-to-authenticator-types">guide to Authenticator Types</a>.</p>
<h3>Assumptions</h3>
<p>The following assumptions have been applied for the development of this authentication assurance standard.</p>
<ul>
<li>For practical purposes, an Authenticator will normally be paired with an identifier that enables look-up of corresponding entity information. This standard assumes an authentication challenge will be a one-to-one comparison (not one-to-many).</li>
<li>Combining 2 or more authentication factors of the same type can add some additional strength in mitigating a threat but does not reduce the overall risk. The authentication assurance strength is determined by the best instance of the authentication factor type.</li>
<li>Authentication combining 3 different authentication factors is possible, but the extra effort does not significantly improve on the strength obtained by the 2 strongest factors.</li>
</ul>
<p>In general, Authenticators and strength are related as follows:</p>
<ul>
<li>LoAA1 can be achieved using a single factor Authenticator with few controls</li>
<li>LoAA2 using a single factor Authenticator with some additional controls.</li>
<li>LoAA3 using a good biometric factor or combining two different factor types in the Authenticator.</li>
<li>LoAA4 using two different factor types where one is a biometric factor implemented with liveness checking.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Document structure</h3>
<p>This standard divides requirements into 2 sections:</p>
<ul>
<li>Requirements for Authentication — these controls apply regardless of the Authenticators used.</li>
<li>Requirements for Authenticator strength by factor — these controls will be applied depending on the type of authentication factors the Authenticators use.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Requirements for Authentication</h2>
<h3>Objective 1 — Authentication risk is understood</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>For entities to trust that their information is being adequately protected from unauthorised access and use, the authentication level should be consistent with the risk posed.</p>
<p>Relying parties may also need to achieve specific levels of assurance to mitigate risks and potentially to comply with legislation.</p>
<h4>AA1.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST carry out an assessment of the authentication risk posed by any service before offering it.</p>
<p>Additional information — While any risk assessment process can be used, specific guidance is available on <a href="https://www.digital.govt.nz/standards-and-guidance/identity/identification-management/guidance/assessing-identification-risk">Assessing identification risk</a>, of which authentication is a part.</p>
<h3>Objective 2 — Ensure correct Authenticator holder behaviour</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>Under normal conditions most Authenticator holders will act appropriately, and directive controls can be relatively effective. Penalties can also discourage incorrect behaviour.</p>
<p>However, Authenticator holders might not initially be aware of their obligations, so these need to be communicated. Over time, understanding may diminish, and ongoing reminders may be appropriate.</p>
<p>At the higher levels of assurance, two-factor authentication helps enforce correct behaviour, so too does detecting behaviour that is not normal in the authentication process.</p>
<p>The RP needs to support correct behaviour by providing the means for the Authenticator holder to report loss or compromise of an Authenticator and appropriately manage the loss of control.</p>
<h4>AA2.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST issue terms and conditions describing the authenticator holder’s obligations, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>the Authenticator is for the sole use of the Authenticator holder</li>
<li>explaining how the holder will keep the Authenticator safe</li>
<li>that the holder reports loss of the Authenticator including unauthorised use, sharing, theft of the Authenticator, possible compromise, or any other suspected loss of control of the Authenticator.</li>
</ul>
<p>Additional information — Examples of expected behaviours:</p>
<ul>
<li>an access card should not be shared with another employee</li>
<li>a passport should remain in the traveller’s possession</li>
<li>or a device provided by the Authenticator holder (such as a mobile phone) can only be used as an Authenticator when it’s individually possessed and used by the holder.</li>
</ul>
<h4>AA2.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST provide communication to Authenticator holders reminding them about their obligations, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>the Authenticator is for the sole use of the holder</li>
<li>the holder will keep the Authenticator safe</li>
<li>that the holder reports loss of the Authenticator including unauthorised use, sharing, theft of the Authenticator, possible compromise, or any other suspected loss of control of the Authenticator.</li>
</ul>
<h4>AA2.03 Control</h4>
<p>The RP limits the ability to share an Authenticator by implementing 2 different factor types.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake this control, unless a biometric factor is used.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control using a biometric factor as 1 of the factors.</p>
<h4>AA2.04 Control</h4>
<p>The RP allows no more than 30 consecutive unsuccessful attempts to authenticate by any factor, disables the account and triggers further investigation.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP SHOULD apply this control.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST apply this control.</p>
<p>Additional information — This control limits the total attempts by an attacker for any single challenge or combination of challenges of more than 1 authentication factor type. This upper limit applies to prevent multiple attempts that are only partially mitigated by subsequent controls such as the 30-minute timeout after a maximum of 5 incorrect attempts.</p>
<p>Where appropriate to the implementation, the RP MAY allow up to 3 re-entries for the same challenge attempt, for example the same received code for the code receiver method.</p>
<h4>AA2.05 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST provide the means for the holder to report loss or compromise of an Authenticator, and can either:</p>
<ul>
<li>deregister the Authenticator and support a process for reregistration; or</li>
<li>if appropriate, close the associated account and require reenrolment.</li>
</ul>
<p>Additional information — Where a biometric factor is used and compromise was not prevented by presentation attack detection, disabling needs to include deregistering as the biometric characteristic cannot be revoked.</p>
<h3>Objective 3 – Entity binding and Authenticator strength are consistent</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>An Authenticator can be established during enrolment or later during a subsequent transaction. In either case it is essential to ensure that the Entity has been bound to the Entity Information at the required level of assurance before attempting to bind an Authenticator.</p>
<p>If there has been a disruption in the binding transaction this will necessitate repeating Entity Binding when the transaction is resumed.</p>
<h4>AA3.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST ensure that, before a new Authenticator is established, the connection between the Entity and their Entity Information is reestablished in the same transaction session by:</p>
<ul>
<li>repeating Entity Binding; or</li>
<li>authentication with an existing Authenticator.</li>
</ul>
<p>Additional information — The existing Authenticator needs to be at an equal or greater level than the new Authenticator being added. If Entity Binding does not achieve the same level as the original Entity Binding a new lower level of Entity Binding is recorded.</p>
<h4>AA3.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST ensure the strength of the Authenticator is consistent with the level of binding assurance (BA) required.</p>
<p>Additional information – Any strength perceived to be gained by using an Authenticator of a higher level of assurance is negated when the corresponding Entity Binding assurance is lower.</p>
<h3>Objective 4 - Entity can control Authenticator</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>Associating an Authenticator with Entity Information without first ensuring that the Entity has control of it, can result in an inability for it to be used by the Entity in a future authentication event or increases the risk of coercion and impersonation.</p>
<h4>AA4.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST ensure that the Entity can respond to all the Authenticator’s challenges before the Authenticator is recorded as active in Entity Information.</p>
<p>Additional information – Depending on the implementation there may be a need to record the existence of the Authenticator in Entity Information before the challenges can be tested. However, the Authenticator will not be available as a recognition mechanism until successful completion of the challenges.</p>
<h4>AA4.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP establishes if the Authenticator has been previously compromised to the extent it makes it unusable.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 – The control does not apply</p>
<p>For level 3 – The RP SHOULD check for compromise with Authenticator issuers or equivalent service providers.</p>
<p>For level 4 – The RP MUST check for compromise with Authenticator issuers or equivalent service providers.</p>
<h3>Objective 5 - Authenticator registration status is maintained</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>Authenticators have lifecycles distinct from the Entity and Entity Information. Authenticators can be reused in multiple contexts, therefore connected to different instances of Entity Information. The Authenticator Registration status provides information to the authentication process as to whether an Authenticator should be accepted, even if the responses to challenges are successful. Typical statuses can include: active, suspended, expired and revoked.</p>
<h4>AA5.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST record enough information in Entity Information for an Authenticator to be recognised and its Authenticator Registration status to be managed.</p>
<h4>AA5.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST be able to update the Authenticator Registration status to prevent authentication occurring, even if the responses to challenges are successful.</p>
<h4>AA5.03 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST NOT accept an authentication event as successful unless the Authenticator Registration status allows.</p>
<h4>AA5.04 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST be able to set an expiry on an Authenticator Registration where the implementation indicates this to be desirable.</p>
<h3>Objective 6 – Authentication events can be investigated</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>An important element of trust in any identification process is the ability for an Entity or Relying Party to question a process or presentation.</p>
<h4>AA6.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST record appropriate detail about the Authenticator establishment process to enable queries or investigation in the future.</p>
<h4>AA6.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST store appropriate detail about an authentication event to enable queries or investigation in the future.</p>
<h2>Requirements for Authenticator strength by factor</h2>
<h3>Objective 7 — Protect knowledge factor response from being guessed or discovered</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>An unauthorised entity can obtain control of a knowledge factor by providing the response that the challenger expects. This threat is most significant when the expected response is static, as once obtained it can be used for multiple authentications. If an expected response is dynamic, then the correct initial response cannot be reused for a subsequent authentication.</p>
<p>Widespread attacks across many Authenticators utilise some form of guessing which may follow sequences, patterns, lists such as dictionaries, or similar techniques.</p>
<p>Targeted attacks on a few Authenticators may utilise some form of discovery to obtain the possible correct responses such as manipulating the holder into disclosing the response or using a list of previously compromised list secrets or the underlying key used to generate a response.</p>
<p>Limiting the number of unsuccessful attempts within a time period is an effective way of controlling automated guessing attacks.</p>
<p>These controls apply where a knowledge factor is used. The controls for replicating the codes related to non-physical challenges on possession factors are covered under Objective 5.</p>
<h4>AA7.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP implements minimum levels of complexity on any knowledge factor response (secret).</p>
<p>For level 1 and 3 — The RP MUST require a minimum complexity of 4 numeric characters or utilise an equivalent level of complexity for responses such as swiping points, matching pictograms.</p>
<p>For level 2 and 4 — The RP MUST require a minimum complexity of:</p>
<ul>
<li>12 characters; or</li>
<li>7 characters from at least 3 of the lower case, upper case, numeric and symbol character sets; or</li>
<li>an equivalent level of complexity for responses such as swiping points, matching pictograms, security questions.</li>
</ul>
<p>Additional information — Upper limits on characters should be set high enough to encourage the use of memorable phrases.</p>
<h4>AA7.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP limits the creation of easily guessable knowledge factor responses by disallowing repetition or patterns and where the Authenticator has the form of an online password, apply the following exclusions (as applicable to the character sets being used):</p>
<ul>
<li>disallow repetitive or sequential characters</li>
<li>disallow specific words — for example, an identifier, username, name of the service</li>
<li>disallow singular dictionary words and common character substitutions</li>
<li>disallow passwords contained in deny lists (usually include overly common combinations and compromised passwords).</li>
</ul>
<p>For level 1 and 3 — The RP SHOULD undertake this control.</p>
<p>For level 2 and 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<p>Additional information — These controls are best implemented using a strength meter during knowledge factor establishment.</p>
<h4>AA7.03 Control</h4>
<p>The RP implements maximum limits for unsuccessful attempts and prevents further attempts for a minimum period.</p>
<p>For level 1 — The RP SHOULD limit unsuccessful attempts to 10 and further attempts for 15 minutes minimum.</p>
<p>For level 2 and above — The RP MUST limit unsuccessful attempts to 5 and disallow further attempts for 30 minutes minimum.</p>
<p>Additional information — In some circumstances, it may be reasonable for the RP to rely on the time and effort taken to provide a response — such as entering a PIN code, as a default control against guessing.</p>
<h4>AA7.04 Control</h4>
<p>The RP prevents use of a guessed or discovered knowledge factor by combining it with an authentication factor of another type.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control using a biometric factor as the second factor.</p>
<p>Additional information – While at level 4 this objective could be met by combining a knowledge factor with a possession factor, it has been restricted to a biometric factor to be consistent with the need for that combination in other level 4 controls.</p>
<h3>Objective 8 — Prevent use of a physically acquired possession factor</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>An Authenticator may be compromised by being physically acquired by someone else.</p>
<p>Possession factors can be acquired by another entity as occasional unauthorised usage or permanent theft.</p>
<p>Where a possession factor is a physical item, the Authenticator holder can become aware that it has been stolen. Requirements for non-physical challenges on possessions and biometric characteristics are covered under Objective 5.</p>
<p>This control applies where a possession factor is used.</p>
<h4>AA8.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP prevents use of a physically acquired possession factor by combining it with an authentication factor of another type.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply. Controls in Objective 2 serve.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control using a biometric factor as the second factor.</p>
<p>Additional information — This objective could be met by combining a possession with a knowledge factor. However, the level 4 requirement has been restricted to a biometric factor to be consistent with the need for this combination in other level 4 controls.</p>
<h3>Objective 9 — Protecting against replication, forgery, or spoofing of possession and biometric factors</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>Authenticators need to be protected against replication, forgery or spoofing by an attacker including the ability to provide the expected static response or 1 or more dynamic responses.</p>
<p>Knowledge-based Authenticators have been covered in Objectives 3 and 4.</p>
<p>Threats against possession-based Authenticators can take the following forms:</p>
<ul>
<li>replication or forgery of documents or devices that must be physically presented for manual or automated challenge</li>
<li>replication of the codes (static or dynamic) used to respond to non-physical challenges on possession of a document, device or software</li>
<li>replication of the value that represents existence in a specific location.</li>
</ul>
<p>The RP needs to ensure that Authenticators based on biometric factors are protected against presentation by another entity (spoofing), including the construction of the expected static response, cloning of 1 or more live responses, or the means to produce all expected live responses.</p>
<p>Some level of protection is provided due to the effort required to undertake successful replication or forgery of a possession factor or spoofing of a biometric.</p>
<p>The requirement for two-factor authentication that protects against physical acquisition at higher levels of assurance also mitigates replication of the expected responses to possession factor challenges.</p>
<p>These controls apply where possession and biometric factors are used.</p>
<h4>AA9.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST protect against replication or forgery of a physically presented Authenticator by incorporating features that ensure the cost of doing so is relative to the level of assurance.</p>
<h4>AA9.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP uses dynamic, non-predictable responses to non-physical challenges on possession factors and limits the response validity to a maximum of 10 minutes or 1 minute, where little messaging delay exists.</p>
<p>For level 1 — The RP MAY undertake this control.</p>
<p>For level 2 and above — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<p>Additional information — The limits need to be sufficiently short to reduce malicious reuse and sufficiently long to be useable by the holder. They can be influenced by the holder group (for example, technologically savvy versus challenged) and the type of Authenticator (for example, code receiver versus code generator).</p>
<h4>AA9.03 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST, for responses to non-physical challenges on possession factors, utilise a minimum complexity of:</p>
<ul>
<li>6 numeric characters; or</li>
<li>4 alphanumeric characters; or</li>
<li>an equivalent level for other codes such as pictograms.</li>
</ul>
<p>Additional information — For usability or avoidance of inappropriate words, some alphanumeric characters MAY be restricted when generating the received codes.</p>
<h4>AA9.04 Control</h4>
<p>The RP addresses spoofing of biometric challenges by ensuring the biometric response is obtained from the Entity using appropriate measures to detect spoofing attempts (for example, recordings, masks, makeup or prosthetics).</p>
<p>For level 1 — The RP SHOULD undertake this control.</p>
<p>For level 2 and above — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<p>Additional information — This control can also help reduce the occurrence of false acceptance of biometric comparisons when spoofing attempts are successfully recognised.</p>
<h4>AA9.05 Control</h4>
<p>The RP obtains biometric factor samples in person or remotely incorporating liveness checking which demonstrates at least 90% resistance to presentation attacks.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake this control, if no other factor is being used.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<h3>Objective 10 — Managing biometric factor probability</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>Biometric characteristics suitable for authentication are substantively unique to individual entities. Therefore, an Authenticator with a biometric factor challenge is potentially a more reliable means of authenticating a specific entity than a knowledge or possession factor. However, unlike the other 2 factor types, a biometric response is probabilistic rather than binary.</p>
<p>There remains the possibility that a manual or systematic comparison will incorrectly match a biometric response from another entity with that of the enrolled entity, resulting in a false positive response to the challenge.</p>
<p>At lower levels of assurance, false positives for a biometric factor challenge should be less than the unmitigated risks for knowledge or possession factor challenges.</p>
<p>There are no additional controls for the lower levels and the RP will need to accept that a small proportion of false positive results may be received.</p>
<p>For higher levels of assurance, an Authenticator with a biometric factor needs to have a very low false positive rate and be used in combination with another authentication factor to protect against the statistical possibility of incorrect authentication.</p>
<h4>AA10.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP reduces the occurrence of false positives in biometric comparisons by using:</p>
<ul>
<li>manual comparison of the biometric characteristic by a trained operator</li>
<li>systematic comparison with a rate of &lt;0.01% false positives, based on a one-to-one comparison.</li>
</ul>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake the control using 1 of the ways stated</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST use systematic comparison.</p>
<p>Additional information — At level 4 manual comparison may be used, however, it needs to be supported by systematic comparison.</p>
<h4>AA10.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP protects against the probabilistic nature of biometric comparisons by combining it with an authentication factor of another type.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake this control, when using manual comparison.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<h2>Contact</h2>
<p>Government Digital Delivery Agency (GDDA)<br>Email: <a href="mailto:idmstandards@gdda.govt.nz">idmstandards@gdda.govt.nz</a></p>

<h2>Requirements for Authentication</h2>
<h3>Objective 1 — Authentication risk is understood</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>For entities to trust that their information is being adequately protected from unauthorised access and use, the authentication level should be consistent with the risk posed.</p>
<p>Relying parties may also need to achieve specific levels of assurance to mitigate risks and potentially to comply with legislation.</p>
<h4>AA1.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST carry out an assessment of the authentication risk posed by any service before offering it.</p>
<p>Additional information — While any risk assessment process can be used, specific guidance is available on <a href="https://www.digital.govt.nz/standards-and-guidance/identity/identification-management/guidance/assessing-identification-risk">Assessing identification risk</a>, of which authentication is a part.</p>
<h3>Objective 2 — Ensure correct Authenticator holder behaviour</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>Under normal conditions most Authenticator holders will act appropriately, and directive controls can be relatively effective. Penalties can also discourage incorrect behaviour.</p>
<p>However, Authenticator holders might not initially be aware of their obligations, so these need to be communicated. Over time, understanding may diminish, and ongoing reminders may be appropriate.</p>
<p>At the higher levels of assurance, two-factor authentication helps enforce correct behaviour, so too does detecting behaviour that is not normal in the authentication process.</p>
<p>The RP needs to support correct behaviour by providing the means for the Authenticator holder to report loss or compromise of an Authenticator and appropriately manage the loss of control.</p>
<h4>AA2.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST issue terms and conditions describing the authenticator holder’s obligations, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>the Authenticator is for the sole use of the Authenticator holder</li>
<li>explaining how the holder will keep the Authenticator safe</li>
<li>that the holder reports loss of the Authenticator including unauthorised use, sharing, theft of the Authenticator, possible compromise, or any other suspected loss of control of the Authenticator.</li>
</ul>
<p>Additional information — Examples of expected behaviours:</p>
<ul>
<li>an access card should not be shared with another employee</li>
<li>a passport should remain in the traveller’s possession</li>
<li>or a device provided by the Authenticator holder (such as a mobile phone) can only be used as an Authenticator when it’s individually possessed and used by the holder.</li>
</ul>
<h4>AA2.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST provide communication to Authenticator holders reminding them about their obligations, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>the Authenticator is for the sole use of the holder</li>
<li>the holder will keep the Authenticator safe</li>
<li>that the holder reports loss of the Authenticator including unauthorised use, sharing, theft of the Authenticator, possible compromise, or any other suspected loss of control of the Authenticator.</li>
</ul>
<h4>AA2.03 Control</h4>
<p>The RP limits the ability to share an Authenticator by implementing 2 different factor types.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake this control, unless a biometric factor is used.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control using a biometric factor as 1 of the factors.</p>
<h4>AA2.04 Control</h4>
<p>The RP allows no more than 30 consecutive unsuccessful attempts to authenticate by any factor, disables the account and triggers further investigation.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP SHOULD apply this control.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST apply this control.</p>
<p>Additional information — This control limits the total attempts by an attacker for any single challenge or combination of challenges of more than 1 authentication factor type. This upper limit applies to prevent multiple attempts that are only partially mitigated by subsequent controls such as the 30-minute timeout after a maximum of 5 incorrect attempts.</p>
<p>Where appropriate to the implementation, the RP MAY allow up to 3 re-entries for the same challenge attempt, for example the same received code for the code receiver method.</p>
<h4>AA2.05 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST provide the means for the holder to report loss or compromise of an Authenticator, and can either:</p>
<ul>
<li>deregister the Authenticator and support a process for reregistration; or</li>
<li>if appropriate, close the associated account and require reenrolment.</li>
</ul>
<p>Additional information — Where a biometric factor is used and compromise was not prevented by presentation attack detection, disabling needs to include deregistering as the biometric characteristic cannot be revoked.</p>
<h3>Objective 3 – Entity binding and Authenticator strength are consistent</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>An Authenticator can be established during enrolment or later during a subsequent transaction. In either case it is essential to ensure that the Entity has been bound to the Entity Information at the required level of assurance before attempting to bind an Authenticator.</p>
<p>If there has been a disruption in the binding transaction this will necessitate repeating Entity Binding when the transaction is resumed.</p>
<h4>AA3.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST ensure that, before a new Authenticator is established, the connection between the Entity and their Entity Information is reestablished in the same transaction session by:</p>
<ul>
<li>repeating Entity Binding; or</li>
<li>authentication with an existing Authenticator.</li>
</ul>
<p>Additional information — The existing Authenticator needs to be at an equal or greater level than the new Authenticator being added. If Entity Binding does not achieve the same level as the original Entity Binding a new lower level of Entity Binding is recorded.</p>
<h4>AA3.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST ensure the strength of the Authenticator is consistent with the level of binding assurance (BA) required.</p>
<p>Additional information – Any strength perceived to be gained by using an Authenticator of a higher level of assurance is negated when the corresponding Entity Binding assurance is lower.</p>
<h3>Objective 4 - Entity can control Authenticator</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>Associating an Authenticator with Entity Information without first ensuring that the Entity has control of it, can result in an inability for it to be used by the Entity in a future authentication event or increases the risk of coercion and impersonation.</p>
<h4>AA4.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST ensure that the Entity can respond to all the Authenticator’s challenges before the Authenticator is recorded as active in Entity Information.</p>
<p>Additional information – Depending on the implementation there may be a need to record the existence of the Authenticator in Entity Information before the challenges can be tested. However, the Authenticator will not be available as a recognition mechanism until successful completion of the challenges.</p>
<h4>AA4.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP establishes if the Authenticator has been previously compromised to the extent it makes it unusable.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 – The control does not apply</p>
<p>For level 3 – The RP SHOULD check for compromise with Authenticator issuers or equivalent service providers.</p>
<p>For level 4 – The RP MUST check for compromise with Authenticator issuers or equivalent service providers.</p>
<h3>Objective 5 - Authenticator registration status is maintained</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>Authenticators have lifecycles distinct from the Entity and Entity Information. Authenticators can be reused in multiple contexts, therefore connected to different instances of Entity Information. The Authenticator Registration status provides information to the authentication process as to whether an Authenticator should be accepted, even if the responses to challenges are successful. Typical statuses can include: active, suspended, expired and revoked.</p>
<h4>AA5.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST record enough information in Entity Information for an Authenticator to be recognised and its Authenticator Registration status to be managed.</p>
<h4>AA5.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST be able to update the Authenticator Registration status to prevent authentication occurring, even if the responses to challenges are successful.</p>
<h4>AA5.03 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST NOT accept an authentication event as successful unless the Authenticator Registration status allows.</p>
<h4>AA5.04 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST be able to set an expiry on an Authenticator Registration where the implementation indicates this to be desirable.</p>
<h3>Objective 6 – Authentication events can be investigated</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>An important element of trust in any identification process is the ability for an Entity or Relying Party to question a process or presentation.</p>
<h4>AA6.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST record appropriate detail about the Authenticator establishment process to enable queries or investigation in the future.</p>
<h4>AA6.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST store appropriate detail about an authentication event to enable queries or investigation in the future.</p>
<h2>Requirements for Authenticator strength by factor</h2>
<h3>Objective 7 — Protect knowledge factor response from being guessed or discovered</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>An unauthorised entity can obtain control of a knowledge factor by providing the response that the challenger expects. This threat is most significant when the expected response is static, as once obtained it can be used for multiple authentications. If an expected response is dynamic, then the correct initial response cannot be reused for a subsequent authentication.</p>
<p>Widespread attacks across many Authenticators utilise some form of guessing which may follow sequences, patterns, lists such as dictionaries, or similar techniques.</p>
<p>Targeted attacks on a few Authenticators may utilise some form of discovery to obtain the possible correct responses such as manipulating the holder into disclosing the response or using a list of previously compromised list secrets or the underlying key used to generate a response.</p>
<p>Limiting the number of unsuccessful attempts within a time period is an effective way of controlling automated guessing attacks.</p>
<p>These controls apply where a knowledge factor is used. The controls for replicating the codes related to non-physical challenges on possession factors are covered under Objective 5.</p>
<h4>AA7.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP implements minimum levels of complexity on any knowledge factor response (secret).</p>
<p>For level 1 and 3 — The RP MUST require a minimum complexity of 4 numeric characters or utilise an equivalent level of complexity for responses such as swiping points, matching pictograms.</p>
<p>For level 2 and 4 — The RP MUST require a minimum complexity of:</p>
<ul>
<li>12 characters; or</li>
<li>7 characters from at least 3 of the lower case, upper case, numeric and symbol character sets; or</li>
<li>an equivalent level of complexity for responses such as swiping points, matching pictograms, security questions.</li>
</ul>
<p>Additional information — Upper limits on characters should be set high enough to encourage the use of memorable phrases.</p>
<h4>AA7.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP limits the creation of easily guessable knowledge factor responses by disallowing repetition or patterns and where the Authenticator has the form of an online password, apply the following exclusions (as applicable to the character sets being used):</p>
<ul>
<li>disallow repetitive or sequential characters</li>
<li>disallow specific words — for example, an identifier, username, name of the service</li>
<li>disallow singular dictionary words and common character substitutions</li>
<li>disallow passwords contained in deny lists (usually include overly common combinations and compromised passwords).</li>
</ul>
<p>For level 1 and 3 — The RP SHOULD undertake this control.</p>
<p>For level 2 and 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<p>Additional information — These controls are best implemented using a strength meter during knowledge factor establishment.</p>
<h4>AA7.03 Control</h4>
<p>The RP implements maximum limits for unsuccessful attempts and prevents further attempts for a minimum period.</p>
<p>For level 1 — The RP SHOULD limit unsuccessful attempts to 10 and further attempts for 15 minutes minimum.</p>
<p>For level 2 and above — The RP MUST limit unsuccessful attempts to 5 and disallow further attempts for 30 minutes minimum.</p>
<p>Additional information — In some circumstances, it may be reasonable for the RP to rely on the time and effort taken to provide a response — such as entering a PIN code, as a default control against guessing.</p>
<h4>AA7.04 Control</h4>
<p>The RP prevents use of a guessed or discovered knowledge factor by combining it with an authentication factor of another type.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control using a biometric factor as the second factor.</p>
<p>Additional information – While at level 4 this objective could be met by combining a knowledge factor with a possession factor, it has been restricted to a biometric factor to be consistent with the need for that combination in other level 4 controls.</p>
<h3>Objective 8 — Prevent use of a physically acquired possession factor</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>An Authenticator may be compromised by being physically acquired by someone else.</p>
<p>Possession factors can be acquired by another entity as occasional unauthorised usage or permanent theft.</p>
<p>Where a possession factor is a physical item, the Authenticator holder can become aware that it has been stolen. Requirements for non-physical challenges on possessions and biometric characteristics are covered under Objective 5.</p>
<p>This control applies where a possession factor is used.</p>
<h4>AA8.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP prevents use of a physically acquired possession factor by combining it with an authentication factor of another type.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply. Controls in Objective 2 serve.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control using a biometric factor as the second factor.</p>
<p>Additional information — This objective could be met by combining a possession with a knowledge factor. However, the level 4 requirement has been restricted to a biometric factor to be consistent with the need for this combination in other level 4 controls.</p>
<h3>Objective 9 — Protecting against replication, forgery, or spoofing of possession and biometric factors</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>Authenticators need to be protected against replication, forgery or spoofing by an attacker including the ability to provide the expected static response or 1 or more dynamic responses.</p>
<p>Knowledge-based Authenticators have been covered in Objectives 3 and 4.</p>
<p>Threats against possession-based Authenticators can take the following forms:</p>
<ul>
<li>replication or forgery of documents or devices that must be physically presented for manual or automated challenge</li>
<li>replication of the codes (static or dynamic) used to respond to non-physical challenges on possession of a document, device or software</li>
<li>replication of the value that represents existence in a specific location.</li>
</ul>
<p>The RP needs to ensure that Authenticators based on biometric factors are protected against presentation by another entity (spoofing), including the construction of the expected static response, cloning of 1 or more live responses, or the means to produce all expected live responses.</p>
<p>Some level of protection is provided due to the effort required to undertake successful replication or forgery of a possession factor or spoofing of a biometric.</p>
<p>The requirement for two-factor authentication that protects against physical acquisition at higher levels of assurance also mitigates replication of the expected responses to possession factor challenges.</p>
<p>These controls apply where possession and biometric factors are used.</p>
<h4>AA9.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST protect against replication or forgery of a physically presented Authenticator by incorporating features that ensure the cost of doing so is relative to the level of assurance.</p>
<h4>AA9.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP uses dynamic, non-predictable responses to non-physical challenges on possession factors and limits the response validity to a maximum of 10 minutes or 1 minute, where little messaging delay exists.</p>
<p>For level 1 — The RP MAY undertake this control.</p>
<p>For level 2 and above — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<p>Additional information — The limits need to be sufficiently short to reduce malicious reuse and sufficiently long to be useable by the holder. They can be influenced by the holder group (for example, technologically savvy versus challenged) and the type of Authenticator (for example, code receiver versus code generator).</p>
<h4>AA9.03 Control</h4>
<p>The RP MUST, for responses to non-physical challenges on possession factors, utilise a minimum complexity of:</p>
<ul>
<li>6 numeric characters; or</li>
<li>4 alphanumeric characters; or</li>
<li>an equivalent level for other codes such as pictograms.</li>
</ul>
<p>Additional information — For usability or avoidance of inappropriate words, some alphanumeric characters MAY be restricted when generating the received codes.</p>
<h4>AA9.04 Control</h4>
<p>The RP addresses spoofing of biometric challenges by ensuring the biometric response is obtained from the Entity using appropriate measures to detect spoofing attempts (for example, recordings, masks, makeup or prosthetics).</p>
<p>For level 1 — The RP SHOULD undertake this control.</p>
<p>For level 2 and above — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<p>Additional information — This control can also help reduce the occurrence of false acceptance of biometric comparisons when spoofing attempts are successfully recognised.</p>
<h4>AA9.05 Control</h4>
<p>The RP obtains biometric factor samples in person or remotely incorporating liveness checking which demonstrates at least 90% resistance to presentation attacks.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake this control, if no other factor is being used.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
<h3>Objective 10 — Managing biometric factor probability</h3>
<h4>Rationale</h4>
<p>Biometric characteristics suitable for authentication are substantively unique to individual entities. Therefore, an Authenticator with a biometric factor challenge is potentially a more reliable means of authenticating a specific entity than a knowledge or possession factor. However, unlike the other 2 factor types, a biometric response is probabilistic rather than binary.</p>
<p>There remains the possibility that a manual or systematic comparison will incorrectly match a biometric response from another entity with that of the enrolled entity, resulting in a false positive response to the challenge.</p>
<p>At lower levels of assurance, false positives for a biometric factor challenge should be less than the unmitigated risks for knowledge or possession factor challenges.</p>
<p>There are no additional controls for the lower levels and the RP will need to accept that a small proportion of false positive results may be received.</p>
<p>For higher levels of assurance, an Authenticator with a biometric factor needs to have a very low false positive rate and be used in combination with another authentication factor to protect against the statistical possibility of incorrect authentication.</p>
<h4>AA10.01 Control</h4>
<p>The RP reduces the occurrence of false positives in biometric comparisons by using:</p>
<ul>
<li>manual comparison of the biometric characteristic by a trained operator</li>
<li>systematic comparison with a rate of &lt;0.01% false positives, based on a one-to-one comparison.</li>
</ul>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake the control using 1 of the ways stated</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST use systematic comparison.</p>
<p>Additional information — At level 4 manual comparison may be used, however, it needs to be supported by systematic comparison.</p>
<h4>AA10.02 Control</h4>
<p>The RP protects against the probabilistic nature of biometric comparisons by combining it with an authentication factor of another type.</p>
<p>For level 1 and 2 — This control does not apply.</p>
<p>For level 3 — The RP MUST undertake this control, when using manual comparison.</p>
<p>For level 4 — The RP MUST undertake this control.</p>
